content.intro: This lesson covers Using Benchmark Results to Guide Optimization. It sits in Module 23, Compiler, Build System, and Performance, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Using Benchmark Results to Guide Optimization matters when you work with explicit absence and failure paths. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Result<T, E> represents either success (Ok(value)) or failure (Err(error)). Callers can handle an error, propagate it with ?, or deliberately convert it.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Using Benchmark Results to Guide Optimization, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Inspect the compilation pipeline to locate a problem, then measure before optimizing. Release-mode results are different from debug-mode results.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Using Benchmark Results to Guide Optimization guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
